title: Investor Renovation Contractor in Wisconsin | Genstone
metaDescription: Genstone renovates investor property across Wisconsin: Milwaukee duplexes, Madison rentals and Green Bay homes, for flips, BRRRR, 203(k) and REO work.
intro: Wisconsin's investment housing is old, practical and built for hard winters, and that combination decides most rehab budgets before an investor picks a paint color. In Milwaukee, upper-and-lower duplexes and Polish flats make two-unit investing a way of life. In Madison, a tight market and a university leasing calendar shape every rental and flip. In Green Bay, modest west side houses and post-war east side ranches attract steady buyers and renters tied to the region's employers. Across all three, investors run into the same recurring items: lead paint, aging plumbing and wiring, wet basements in clay soils, and exterior work that has to wait for warm weather. Genstone Construction plans and manages renovations for investors, lenders and servicers in Wisconsin from our Romeoville, Illinois headquarters, coordinating vetted, licensed local contractors in each market. Every project begins with a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review, followed by an itemized scope with a draw schedule tied to completed work, a single field manager from start to finish, and no upfront payment. Our work covers fix and flip, BRRRR, rentals, small multifamily, FHA 203(k) and REO.

sections.h2: Wisconsin housing stock and what it means for a rehab
sections.body:
Most Wisconsin investor properties were built either before the Second World War or in the two decades after it, and each era has a predictable list of rehab items.

The older stock is concentrated in Milwaukee, the near east side of Madison, the west side of Green Bay and the historic cores of smaller cities across the state. Milwaukee is known for its upper-and-lower duplexes, the raised-cottage Polish flats of the south side and houses faced in pale cream city brick. Older homes in these areas usually have balloon framing, plaster walls, stone or brick foundations, galvanized water lines, cast-iron drains, knob-and-tube wiring and lead paint on nearly every painted surface. Porches and chimneys take a beating from freeze-thaw cycles.

Post-war neighborhoods, such as Madison's west side, Green Bay's east side and Milwaukee's outer edges, are filled with Cape Cods, ranches and split-levels on block or poured foundations. These houses are simpler to renovate but often contain asbestos in floor tile, mastic and duct wrap, original electrical panels and aging sewer laterals.

Across the state, heavy clay soils and spring snowmelt make basement water one of the most common problems, and long winters make attic insulation and heating reliability central to any rental or resale plan. A good Wisconsin scope prices these items before closing, not after demolition.

Each of Genstone's Wisconsin markets favors different strategies.

Milwaukee is the state's deepest market for small multifamily and buy-and-hold investing. Duplexes are everywhere in the older neighborhoods, from Sherman Park and Washington Heights to Bay View and the south side, which gives investors a large pool to buy from and an appraiser pool accustomed to valuing two-unit income property. Flips perform best where owner-occupants compete, such as Bay View, parts of Riverwest and the neighborhoods near Wauwatosa. The city also has a long-running supply of tax-foreclosed and bank-owned houses, keeping REO work steady.

Madison is a high-demand, high-price market. Rentals near the University of Wisconsin campus and on the isthmus stay leased, but acquisition prices leave little room for mistakes, so flips and BRRRR projects depend on accurate estimating and finish levels that match recent sales. The August lease turnover near campus dominates the rental renovation calendar.

Green Bay offers moderate prices and steady demand from a stable job base. West side neighborhoods suit rentals and BRRRR, while east side ranches and older homes in the Astor area work well for flips aimed at first-time buyers and families.

In all three markets, the FHA 203(k) program opens doors for owner-occupant buyers purchasing older homes and duplexes that need work, and Genstone, as an FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor, prepares the bids and draw documentation that lenders require.

sections.h2: Permits, codes and licensing in Wisconsin
sections.body:
Wisconsin regulates residential construction at both the state and local level, and investors benefit from understanding the basics.

One- and two-family homes fall under the state's Uniform Dwelling Code, which is administered through local building inspection departments in cities such as Milwaukee, Madison and Green Bay. A contractor who pulls a building permit for work on a one- or two-family dwelling must hold the state's Dwelling Contractor certification, with a certified qualifier responsible for the work. Buildings with three or more units generally fall under the state's commercial building code, which can change design and inspection requirements on triplex and fourplex projects. Trade licenses for electrical, plumbing and HVAC work are issued statewide by the Department of Safety and Professional Services.

Lead-safe renovation is a significant issue in Wisconsin because so much housing predates 1978. Work that disturbs paint in older homes should be done by certified renovators using lead-safe practices, and Wisconsin administers its own lead-safe renovation certification program.

Local rules add another layer. Milwaukee's Department of Neighborhood Services runs a vacant building registration program and issues code orders that follow a property through a sale. Madison has local historic districts where the Landmarks Commission reviews exterior changes. Suburbs run their own building departments with their own procedures. Genstone confirms the jurisdiction for each property and builds permits and inspections into every schedule.

Wisconsin's climate shapes when and how renovation work gets done. Winters are long and cold, with deep frost that heaves porches, steps and slabs without proper footings and pushes on older foundation walls. Ice dams are a familiar problem on homes with poor attic insulation and ventilation, and they drive water into ceilings and walls. Vacant houses are especially vulnerable: when heat fails, pipes freeze and burst, boilers crack, and water spreads through floors and into basements, often followed by mold.

Spring snowmelt and rain saturate clay soils, which is when basements leak the most and when drainage problems become obvious. That makes spring a useful time to see how a basement really behaves before finalizing a scope.

For scheduling, exterior work such as roofing, masonry, tuckpointing, siding, porch rebuilds, concrete and exterior painting fits best between late spring and early fall. Interior work, including kitchens, baths, flooring, plaster repair and mechanical replacements, continues through winter as long as the house is heated and secure. Many investors use the cold months for interior renovations and plan to list or lease in spring.

Genstone builds these seasonal realities into every scope and draw schedule, separating exterior and interior phases so weather affects only the work it should. Winter acquisitions get a plumbing and heating check before finishes are planned.

faqs.q: Which Wisconsin cities does Genstone serve?
faqs.a: Genstone currently plans renovations in Milwaukee, Madison and Green Bay, along with surrounding communities such as Wauwatosa, West Allis, Fitchburg, Sun Prairie, De Pere and Ashwaubenon. We coordinate vetted, licensed local contractors in each market while our estimators, field managers and billing team work from our Romeoville, Illinois headquarters. Contact us about a specific property and we will confirm coverage and begin with a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review.

faqs.q: Does a Wisconsin fourplex follow different code rules than a duplex?
faqs.a: Generally, yes. One- and two-family homes fall under Wisconsin's Uniform Dwelling Code, while buildings with three or more units typically fall under the state's commercial building code. That can affect fire separation, egress, plan review and inspections on triplex and fourplex renovations. We identify which code applies during scoping and plan permits and inspections accordingly, so the budget reflects the right requirements from the start.

faqs.q: How does Genstone handle lead paint in Wisconsin homes?
faqs.a: Because most older Wisconsin housing predates 1978, we plan lead-safe work into scopes from the beginning. Work that disturbs painted surfaces is done using lead-safe practices by certified renovators, and windows, porches and other friction surfaces are addressed as part of the renovation. That approach protects occupants and reduces the risk of later problems with tenants, buyers or local health departments.

faqs.q: How are Wisconsin renovation projects paid for?
faqs.a: Genstone requires no upfront payment. Each project has a draw schedule tied to completed stages of work, which your field manager documents with photos and notes before a draw is requested. The last payment is due only when the work is complete and you have signed off. Dumpster and debris costs are included in every estimate, and Genstone Financial offers fix-and-flip, DSCR rental, line of credit and new construction loans if you want financing within the Genstone Companies.
